records.name: Aino
records.facts_used: Estonian Aino is borrowed from Finnish Aino. Finnish aino is a poetic form of ainoa, only or sole, from which the personal name is explained. It also belongs to the name-world of the Kalevala; similar spelling does not make it the different masculine name Eino. In the feminine-name list of Mägiste’s 1929 Eestipäraseid isikunimesid, Aino appears with related forms and the German gloss die einzige, the only one. This is a specific printed example in an Estonian name collection, not evidence that the name was created in 1929.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact Estonian dictionary entry says borrowed from Finnish Aino; Finnish section and curated guide give aino/ainoa, only/sole, and Kalevala context. Mägiste PDF p. 13 / printed p. 11 visually checked: feminine Aino with related forms and German die einzige. Publication is 1929, not coining. Supplied calendar has Aino on 17 November, while Statistics Estonia’s published list places Aino in the 10 May group and Eino in the 17 November group. Preserve the project date and spelling and record the discrepancy; do not silently replace Aino with Eino.

records.name: Egil
records.facts_used: Egil is connected with Old Norse Egill. Guides give agi, awe or fear, in its old basis; a Norwegian name scholar also discusses respect and a sword’s edge. These dictionary nuances remain explicit rather than becoming one exact translation imposed on every use of the name. The Icelandic Egils saga tells of the skald Egil Skallagrimsson. The encyclopaedia tentatively dates its composition to before 1240 and its main manuscript Möðruvallabók to the first half of the fourteenth century. These date a literary work and manuscript, not Estonian personal-name records of those years.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Curated entry gives Old Norse Egill, agi awe/fear; signed Gulbrand Alhaug article additionally discusses respect and sword edge. Both nuances are retained, not a forced literal translation. Opened SNL Egils saga dates composition tentatively before 1240 and main manuscript Möðruvallabók to the first half of the fourteenth century. Narrative identifies Icelandic literary/manuscript evidence, not an Estonian first attestation or independently verified saga events.

records.name: Egon
records.facts_used: The Estonian dictionary entry identifies Egon as borrowed from German Egon. The international guide explains it through old Egino and the element agin, edge or blade. This is a historical name explanation; resemblance to other Eg- names does not establish identical derivations for them all. Estonian dramatist Egon Rannet was known as Eugen or Jevgeni Brücke until 1940. The university’s writers’ dictionary dates his play Kadunud poeg to 1958. An individual change of name is a biographical fact, not proof that Egon is generally a short form of Eugen.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact Estonian dictionary entry says from German Egon. Curated guide gives Egino/agin, edge or blade; the German Wiktionary section additionally discusses a historical awe/edge merger, not an Eugen derivation. Opened Tartu EWOD biography identifies Egon Rannet as Eugen/Jevgeni Brücke until 1940 and dates Kadunud poeg to 1958. Individual renaming does not establish a general Egon/Eugen etymological rule.

records.name: Einar
records.facts_used: The Estonian dictionary entry derives Einar from Old Norse Einarr. Its historical elements are einn, one or alone, and herr, army or warrior. This explains the structure of a name rather than promise a combative character or solitary life to its bearer. The University of Tartu’s writers’ dictionary dates Einar Maasik’s literary debut in the newspaper Edasi to 1953. His prose collections Koduküla teel (1959) and Teekaaslane (1960) followed. These provide specific examples of the name in Estonian literary history.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact Estonian dictionary entry derives from Old Norse Einarr; curated entry gives einn and herr. Opened University of Tartu EWOD Einar Maasik entry documents Edasi debut 1953, Koduküla teel 1959 and Teekaaslane 1960. An initially guessed Einar Rannut URL returned 404 and was not used.

records.name: Dionyzas
records.facts_used: Salys’s dictionary appendix lists Dionyzas alongside Dionizas with the equivalent Dionysius. This Greek personal-name family is connected with the god Dionysos. The deity’s name is therefore distinguished from the human naming tradition formed from it. The 1983 second volume of Salys’s writings separates the deity entry Dionisas from the personal names Dionyzas and Dionizas. This is a concrete example of a dictionary distinguishing a mythological figure from human names. The volume’s date records republication rather than their first appearance in Lithuania.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Salys PDF p. 224 / printed p. 209 visually checked: separate deity Dionisas and personal names Dionyzas und Dionizas → Dionys(ius). Curated Dionysios connects the personal-name family to Dionysos. LT-GUIDE’s divine tree explanation is explicitly speculative and is not accepted as a verified whole-name translation. Narrative stops at the documented divine-name family rather than inventing its ultimate etymology. The 1983 volume dates republication, not first use. The guessed VLE Dionyzas Poška URL returned 404 and no biography was accepted from it.

records.name: Getautas
records.facts_used: Getautas is a Lithuanian two-stem name. The guide connects ge- with gedauti and gedėti, to long for or mourn, and taut- with tauta, people or nation. These explanations describe separate elements; they need not become one compulsory sentence about someone’s longing or duty towards a nation. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą name calendar places Getautas on 17 November with short form Getas. The list was reprinted in volume two of Salys’s writings in 1983. It documents both the full and proposed short forms, while calendar publication itself does not date the name’s invention.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact LT-GUIDE gives ge- gedauti/gedėti and taut- tauta. Salys PDF p. 317 / printed p. 302 visually checked: Getautas (Getas), 17 November in the 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar, reprinted 1983. No creation date or automatic change of Getautas to Gedautas.

records.name: Salomėja
records.facts_used: Salomėja belongs to a Semitic name family connected with Hebrew shalom, peace. The Lithuanian guide points to Šlomit, while the international reference describes an Aramaic Salome route. The shared basis is peace; these accounts should not be merged into one supposedly proved chain of borrowing. Lithuanian poet Salomėja Nėris published her first poetry collection Anksti rytą in 1927. The encyclopaedia records her first use of the pen name Neris, later Nėris, for Pajūry in the journal Ateitis in 1923. That pen name concerns the surname component, not a new spelling of Salomėja.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact LT-GUIDE gives Šlomit/shalom; curated Salome describes an Aramaic name related to Hebrew shalom. Keep the common peace basis without asserting a unique direct transmission chain. Opened VLE biography confirms Salomėja Nėris’s first collection Anksti rytą 1927 and first pen-name use Neris in Pajūry, Ateitis no. 11, 1923; distinguish the surname pen name from the given name.

records.name: Hugo
records.facts_used: Hugo is a Germanic name based on hugu, mind, thought or spirit. The element Hug- appears in old German personal names. These meanings describe the name’s historical structure rather than predict the abilities or character of every person who bears it. The Siliņš dictionary catalogue dates Hugo’s calendar entry to 1767 and a personal-name record to 1871. Calendar publication and a record of personal use are different kinds of historical evidence. The earlier calendar year neither invalidates the later record nor establishes when the name was invented.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or documented family evidence and a concrete historical, dictionary, bibliographic or literary episode support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact LV-SILINS p. 156: hugu family, calendar 1767 and personal record 1871. Curated Hugh/Hugo entries corroborate mind/thought/spirit; Victor Hugo is a surname, so his biography was not substituted for a first-name record.
